bib.title: Comparing AI Agents to Cybersecurity Professionals in Real-World Penetration Testing

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Comparing AI Agents to Cybersecurity Professionals in Real-World Penetration Testing", Lin, Jones, Jasper, et al. (13 authors). No venue is printed; the PDF carries only "arXiv:2512.09882v2 [cs.AI] 3 Mar 2026", so it is a preprint. First author Justin W. Lin: Stanford University. Other affiliations printed: Carnegie Mellon University, Gray Swan AI. Funding: Stanford HAI seed grant and "an unrestricted gift from OpenAI".

COVERAGE: 29 of 29 pages, 81,884 of 81,884 chars (main text p1-9, ethics p10, appendices A-K p14-29). References p11-13 skimmed. Figures 2-4 extracted as garbled glyphs, so only their captions were read.

CLAIMS

- claim: The human baseline was 10 recruited professionals on a live university network, paid a flat fee.
  number: 10 people; ~8,000 hosts, 12 subnets; $2000 each; at least 10 hours requested
  setup: recruited by referral and community calls, self-reported credentials; identical Kali VM each; student-level account
  quote: "We requested that participants commit at least 10 working hours to the engagement."
  where: p3

- claim: The score sums technical complexity plus a severity weight per valid finding.
  number: weights 8/5/3/2/1 (Critical to Informational); verified-but-not-exploited findings are penalised
  setup: rubric written by the authors "based on industry standards and consultation with the target organization"; research group triaged with IT staff
  quote: "Assessing penetration test quality is inherently subjective."
  where: p3-4; rubric p29

- claim: The authors' scaffold (A2, an ensemble of supervisor models) ranked second of 15 entries.
  number: total score 95.2 against 111.4 for P1; 11 submissions, 82% valid
  setup: one run, first 10 of 16 hours scored
  quote: "ARTEMIS placed second overall, discovering 9 valid vulnerabilities with an 82% valid submission rate and outperforming 9 of 10 human participants."
  where: p1; Table 1 p2

- claim: Scaffold changed the ranking more than model did.
  number: GPT-5 beat 5 of 10 humans in ARTEMIS (A1), 2 in Codex, 0 in CyAgent
  setup: one run each; Codex and CyAgent stopped early
  quote: "A1 outperforms 50% of human participants, yet GPT-5 in Codex outperforms only 2, and GPT-5 in CyAgent is outperformed by all others."
  where: p6

- claim: The cheap configuration is not the one that placed second.
  number: A1 $18.21/hr; A2 $59/hr
  setup: API cost over the full 16-hour window; the human figure is an Indeed salary
  quote: "A1 cost $291.47 ($18.21/hr, or $37,876/year at 40 hours/week). A2 cost $944.07 ($59/hr, $122,720/year)."
  where: p8

- claim: Agents submitted more invalid findings and failed a GUI-dependent task.
  number: A1 55% valid, A2 82%, eight of ten humans 100%; 80% of humans found the GUI-gated finding
  setup: Appendix B lists A1 as 6 valid, 1 duplicate, 4 not valid of 11 (my count)
  quote: "While 80% of participants found a remote code execution vulnerability on a Windows machine accessible via TinyPilot, ARTEMIS struggled with the GUI-based interaction."
  where: p8; Table 1 p2; Appendix B p17-18

- claim: Three scaffolds scored zero for reasons other than capability.
  number: 0 findings each
  setup: Claude Code and MAPTA refused; Incalmo stalled
  quote: "Claude Code and MAPTA refuse the task out of the box, while Incalmo stalls at early reconnaissance due to its rigid task graph, resulting in 0 findings each."
  where: p6

LIMITS
- Conceded by the authors: "logistical constraints limited sample sizes, precluding hypothesis testing with sufficient statistical power" (p8). Also a compressed time frame, and an IT team that knew of the test and manually approved flagged actions.
- No repeated runs and no intervals anywhere. Each agent configuration ran once; the hinted follow-up trials are pass@1. On Cybench the authors themselves put a 48.6% vs 45.9% gap down to "sampling variance".
- The paper gives no single false-positive rate. It reports valid % per entry and a figure.
- No inter-rater agreement, no statement of who assigned severity and complexity scores, and no mention of blinding. The authors scored their own agent.
- The ranking depends on the complexity term. On severity score alone P4 (64) leads, A2 (54) is second and P1 (44) is fourth (my reading of Table 1).
- The headline "$18/hour versus $60/hour" pairs A1's cost with A2's rank. A2 at $59/hr is at parity with the human figure.
- Costs exclude the researcher who watched every agent session and the IT monitor. $60/hour appears only in the abstract.
- Time budgets are inconsistent: "at least 10 working hours" (p3) against "up to 10 hours of active engagement and 4 days of system access" (p8). P1 did reconnaissance before the clock started.
- Not stated: whether agents ran before or after human findings were patched.
- Dated: models are GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4 and Opus 4, o3, Gemini 2.5 Pro.

BUILDS ON: Cybench (Zhang et al., 2025a) and BountyBench (Zhang et al., 2025b), which share authors with this paper; dynamic prompts from Wang et al. [2025b]; model ensembling from Alloy Agents [Ziegler, 2025]; sub-agents forked from OpenAI's Codex; MITRE ATT&CK for categorising techniques.

CODE: none worth keeping. The scoring formula is S_total = sum of (TC_i + W_i), p3.

FIGURES: Figure 3, p6, "Number of valid participant findings over time." It shows humans submitting throughout the window while most agents stop early, which is the time-matching problem at a glance. I did not inspect it visually.

PROBLEMS
- Figures 2-4 are unreadable in extraction, so per-entry false-positive shares from Figure 2 could not be read.
- Eq. 2 extracts as "DCi + (ECi × −0.2)". The negative sign is consistent with A2's 41.2 complexity score in my recomputation from Appendix B, but verified-only findings are not marked there.
- Appendix B has five rows labelled "A0", which is never defined, and no rows for Codex (CO) despite its 7 findings in Table 1.
- Appendices C and J contain imperative text (participant instructions, the agent prompt). It is study material and was treated as data.
